newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Former Bolivian dictator sworn in as president.
newsitem.headline: Former Bolivian dictator sworn in as president.

text.p: Former military dictator Hugo Banzer took office on Wednesday as Bolivia's new president, vowing to defend free market policies and make the fight against poverty his priority.

"Our immediate challenge is to seek economic growth as an inseparable part of human development, giving priority to education, health and stable employment and not threatening the lifestyles of future generations," he said.
Banzer promised at his swearing-in ceremony to deepen a 12-year-old free market drive, but said the failings that have left seven out of 10 Bolivians still living in poverty must be corrected.
"We will never be able to build stability with chronic social strife and disappointment, especially when we are not taking necessary steps to ease the sharp divisions among Bolivians," Banzer said.

Banzer, who ruled Bolivia as dictator from 1971-78, was elected president by Congress on Tuesday after he forged unlikely alliances with leftist and populist parties. Constitutional reforms mean Banzer will be the first elected president to rule for five years instead of four.

Outgoing President Sanchez de Losada, barred from running again, described the transfer of power as only a change in style. "People wanted a president who could impose order. But nobody can deny the Bolivia we are leaving is very different from the one we received four years ago," he said.

Banzer, 71, won general elections on June 1 for the rightist National Democrats. But he failed to get an absolute majority, forcing a second-round vote in Congress against Juan Carlos Duran of the ruling Nationalist Revolutionary Movement.

Banzer also won the popular vote in 1985, but lost to a rival in Congress. This time he allied himself with the Revolutionary Left Movement of ex-President Jaime Paz Zamora and two populist parties, including the Solidarity Civic Union of millionaire Ivo Kuljis.

New Vice President Jorge Quiroga said the priorities would be creating jobs, improving the court system and fighting poverty. He told Reuters that half of the population lacks basic health care, two out of three children do not attend elementary school and 95 percent of the rural population and 50 percent of city dwellers live below the poverty line.
